title: Atoms, moles and bonding: practice questions (AI-written)

questions.question: How many hydrogen atoms are there in 0.250 mol of ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4? [Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1] A: 3.01 x 10^23; B: 6.02 x 10^23; C: 1.20 x 10^24; D: 4.82 x 10^24
steps: Each formula unit of (NH4)2SO4 contains 2 x 4 = 8 hydrogen atoms.
Moles of H atoms = 0.250 x 8 = 2.00 mol, so the number of atoms = 2.00 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.20 x 10^24.
A counts only 2 H per formula unit and B counts only 4. D forgets to multiply by 0.250 mol.

questions.question: Which sample contains the greatest total number of atoms? [Ar: H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0] A: 2.0 g of H2; B: 18 g of H2O; C: 34 g of NH3; D: 16 g of CH4
questions.answer: C: 34 g of NH3
steps: A: 2.0 g of H2 is 1.0 mol of molecules, so 2.0 mol of atoms.
B: 18 g of H2O is 1.0 mol, so 3.0 mol of atoms. D: 16 g of CH4 is 1.0 mol, so 5.0 mol of atoms.
C: 34 g of NH3 is 34 / 17.0 = 2.0 mol, with 4 atoms per molecule, so 8.0 mol of atoms, the greatest.

questions.question: A compound contains 26.6 % potassium, 35.4 % chromium and 38.1 % oxygen by mass. Determine its empirical formula. [Ar: K = 39.1, Cr = 52.0, O = 16.0]
questions.answer: K2Cr2O7
steps: Divide by the smallest (0.680): K : Cr : O = 1 : 1 : 3.5.
Multiply by 2 to give whole numbers, 2 : 2 : 7, so the empirical formula is K2Cr2O7.

questions.question: 0.560 g of a hydrocarbon burns completely in excess oxygen, producing 1.76 g of carbon dioxide and 0.720 g of water. The relative molecular mass of the hydrocarbon is 70.0. Determine its empirical formula and its molecular formula. [Ar: H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0]
questions.answer: Empirical formula CH2; molecular formula C5H10
steps: Moles of CO2 = 1.76 / 44.0 = 0.0400 mol, so moles of C = 0.0400 mol (0.480 g).
Moles of H2O = 0.720 / 18.0 = 0.0400 mol, so moles of H = 0.0800 mol (0.0800 g); 0.480 + 0.0800 = 0.560 g, which confirms there is no oxygen.
C : H = 0.0400 : 0.0800 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH2 (mass 14.0).
Molecular formula: 70.0 / 14.0 = 5, so it is C5H10.

questions.question: A gas has a mass of 0.250 g and occupies a volume of 139 cm^3 at a pressure of 101 kPa and a temperature of 25 degrees C. Use the ideal gas equation to calculate the relative molecular mass of the gas. [R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1]
steps: Convert to SI units: p = 101 000 Pa, V = 139 x 10^-6 m^3 = 1.39 x 10^-4 m^3, T = 298 K.

questions.question: In a blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. (a) A furnace uses 2.50 x 10^3 kg of iron(III) oxide and produces 1.42 x 10^3 kg of iron. Calculate the percentage yield of iron. [Ar: Fe = 55.8, O = 16.0]
steps: Moles of Fe expected = 2 x 1.566 x 10^4 = 3.133 x 10^4 mol, so the theoretical mass = 3.133 x 10^4 x 55.8 = 1.748 x 10^6 g = 1748 kg.
Percentage yield = 1.42 x 10^3 / 1748 x 100 = 81.2 %.

questions.question: In a blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. (b) Calculate the atom economy for the production of iron by this reaction. [Ar: C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Fe = 55.8]
steps: Atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100.
Mass of 2Fe = 111.6. Total mass of reactants = 159.6 + 3(28.0) = 243.6.

questions.question: 2.40 g of magnesium is added to 50.0 cm^3 of 1.00 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. Deduce which reactant is limiting, and calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at room temperature and pressure. [Ar of Mg = 24.3; molar volume of a gas = 24.0 dm^3 mol^-1]
questions.answer: HCl is limiting; 600 cm^3 of hydrogen
steps: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2: 0.0988 mol of Mg would need 0.198 mol of HCl, but only 0.0500 mol is present, so HCl is the limiting reagent.
Moles of H2 = 0.0500 / 2 = 0.0250 mol (from the limiting reagent), so volume = 0.0250 x 24.0 = 0.600 dm^3 = 600 cm^3.

questions.question: Hydrated magnesium sulfate has the formula MgSO4.7H2O. (a) Calculate the percentage by mass of water in MgSO4.7H2O. [Ar: Mg = 24.3, S = 32.1, O = 16.0, H = 1.0]
steps: Percentage of water = 126.0 / 246.4 x 100 = 51.1 %.

questions.question: A student heats 3.69 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO4.xH2O, until a constant mass of 1.80 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains. (b) Determine the value of x. [Mr of MgSO4 = 120.4; Mr of H2O = 18.0]
steps: Mass of water lost = 3.69 - 1.80 = 1.89 g, so moles of H2O = 1.89 / 18.0 = 0.105 mol.
Moles of MgSO4 = 1.80 / 120.4 = 0.01495 mol.

questions.question: In the experiment in (b), the student heats the solid, cools it and reweighs it, and repeats this until the mass no longer changes. (c) Explain why the student heats to constant mass.
questions.answer: To make sure all of the water has been driven off
steps: To make sure that all of the water of crystallisation has been driven off
A constant mass shows no more water is being lost; otherwise the mass of water lost is too small and x is too low
accept: heating repeated until two consecutive masses agree
if the mass is still falling, water remains in the solid
cool in a desiccator so the anhydrous salt does not take up moisture from the air

questions.question: A second student carries out the experiment in (b) and obtains x = 6.4. (d) Suggest one error that could have caused this low value of x, and explain its effect.
questions.answer: Incomplete heating: some water remained, so the mass of water lost is too small and x is too low
steps: Incomplete heating, so some water of crystallisation remained in the solid
The mass of water lost is too small (the mass of anhydrous solid too large), so x is too low
accept: the anhydrous solid absorbed moisture from the air while cooling, giving a residue mass that was too high
the hydrated sample was already partly dehydrated
a balance error giving a residue mass that was too high

questions.question: Which species has the electron configuration 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^5? A: Fe2+; B: Mn2+; C: Cr3+; D: Zn2+
questions.answer: B: Mn2+
steps: The configuration has 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 5 = 23 electrons.
Mn (atomic number 25) loses 2 electrons to form Mn2+ with 23 electrons, [Ar] 3d^5.
A: Fe2+ has 24 electrons (3d^6). C: Cr3+ has 21 electrons (3d^3). D: Zn2+ has 28 electrons (3d^10).

questions.question: Which row gives the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons, in that order, in a chloride ion of the isotope chlorine-37? A: 17, 20, 17; B: 17, 20, 18; C: 17, 37, 18; D: 18, 19, 17
steps: Chlorine has atomic number 17, so there are 17 protons.
Neutrons = mass number - protons = 37 - 17 = 20.
The 1- charge means one extra electron, so 17 + 1 = 18 electrons. A has no extra electron, C gives the mass number as the neutron number, and D has the wrong proton number.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a sample of copper shows two peaks: one at m/z = 63 with a relative abundance of 69.2 and one at m/z = 65 with a relative abundance of 30.8. Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper in this sample, to 3 significant figures.
steps: The height of each peak is the relative abundance of that isotope.
Ar = 63.616, which is 63.6 to 3 s.f.

questions.question: (i) Write the electron configurations of chromium (atomic number 24) and copper (atomic number 29), using the 1s^2 2s^2 ... notation. (ii) Explain why these configurations do not follow the expected filling order.
questions.answer: (i) Cr: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^5 4s^1; Cu: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^10 4s^1; (ii) a half-full or full 3d subshell is more stable
steps: A half-filled (3d^5) or full (3d^10) d subshell is more stable (lower in energy), so one 4s electron moves into 3d
accept: the expected arrangements 3d^4 4s^2 and 3d^9 4s^2 are higher in energy
the 3d and 4s subshells are very close in energy, so little energy is needed to promote an electron

questions.question: The first five ionisation energies of an element X, in kJ mol^-1, are 786, 1577, 3232, 4356 and 16091. (i) Deduce the group of the Periodic Table containing X. (ii) Write the equation, with state symbols, for the third ionisation energy of X.
steps: A very large jump between the fourth and fifth ionisation energies
So there are four electrons in the outer shell: Group 4 (14)
accept: the fifth electron is removed from an inner shell, closer to the nucleus
Group IV or Group 14 accepted
e written without the minus sign accepted

questions.question: The first ionisation energy of oxygen (1314 kJ mol^-1) is lower than that of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol^-1). Explain why.
questions.answer: In oxygen the outer 2p electrons are paired in one orbital and repel, so one is easier to remove than the unpaired 2p electron in nitrogen
steps: The three 2p electrons in nitrogen are unpaired, in separate orbitals
In oxygen two of the 2p electrons are paired in the same orbital and repel each other
So it is easier to remove an electron from oxygen, giving a lower first ionisation energy
accept: pair repulsion in oxygen outweighs its greater nuclear charge
nitrogen has a half-filled p subshell, which is more stable
the electron removed from oxygen comes from a doubly occupied 2p orbital

questions.question: The first ionisation energies of Group 2 elements and of aluminium are: Mg 738, Ca 590 and Al 578 kJ mol^-1. (a) Define the term first ionisation energy.
questions.answer: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms, forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions
steps: The energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms
To form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions
accept: the energy change when one mole of gaseous atoms loses one mole of electrons
X(g) -> X+(g) + e- given as part of the definition
one electron removed from each atom

questions.question: The first ionisation energies of Mg, Ca and Al are 738, 590 and 578 kJ mol^-1. (b) Write the equation, including state symbols, for the first ionisation energy of magnesium.
questions.answer: Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-
steps: Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-
accept: Mg(g) - e- -> Mg+(g)
e written without the minus sign, provided the state symbols (g) are shown

questions.question: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is 738 kJ mol^-1 and that of calcium is 590 kJ mol^-1. (c) Explain why the first ionisation energy of calcium is lower than that of magnesium.
questions.answer: Calcium has an extra shell, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, and is held less strongly
steps: Calcium has an extra electron shell, so a larger atomic radius than magnesium
The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by the inner electrons
The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker, so less energy is needed to remove it
accept: this outweighs the increase in nuclear charge
the outer electron is in the 4s rather than the 3s subshell
ionisation energies decrease down the group

questions.question: The first ionisation energy of aluminium is 578 kJ mol^-1 and that of magnesium is 738 kJ mol^-1. (d) Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
questions.answer: The outer electron of Al is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy and shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily than the 3s electron of Mg
steps: The outer electron of aluminium is in a 3p subshell, but that of magnesium is in 3s
A 3p electron is higher in energy (further from the nucleus) and is shielded by the 3s electrons
So it is easier to remove, despite the greater nuclear charge of aluminium
accept: 3p orbitals have a higher energy than 3s orbitals
the full 3s^2 subshell of magnesium is a stable arrangement

questions.question: Which species has a trigonal pyramidal shape? A: BF3; B: NH4+; C: H3O+; D: CH4
questions.answer: C: H3O+
steps: H3O+ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around oxygen, so it is trigonal pyramidal.
A: BF3 has three bonding pairs and no lone pair, so it is trigonal planar.
B and D: NH4+ and CH4 each have four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so they are tetrahedral.

questions.question: Which molecule contains polar bonds but is not polar overall? A: CHCl3; B: H2O; C: BF3; D: NH3
questions.answer: C: BF3
steps: BF3 is a symmetrical trigonal planar molecule, so the three B-F bond dipoles cancel and there is no overall dipole.
A: CHCl3 is tetrahedral with different atoms, so its dipoles do not cancel. B: H2O is bent and D: NH3 is pyramidal, so both are polar.

questions.question: The bond angle is 109.5 degrees in methane, 107 degrees in ammonia and 104.5 degrees in water. Explain these differences.
questions.answer: All have four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so the angle decreases as the number of lone pairs increases
steps: Electron pairs repel and take up positions of minimum repulsion; CH4, NH3 and H2O each have four electron pairs, arranged tetrahedrally
CH4 has four bonding pairs, which repel equally, giving 109.5 degrees
NH3 has one lone pair, which repels the bonding pairs more than they repel one another, giving 107 degrees
H2O has two lone pairs, so the repulsion is greater still, giving 104.5 degrees
accept: lone pair-lone pair repulsion is greater than lone pair-bonding pair, which is greater than bonding pair-bonding pair repulsion
the bond angle decreases as the number of lone pairs increases
a lone pair occupies more space because it is closer to the central atom

questions.question: Compare the structures of diamond and graphite and explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
questions.answer: Diamond: each C bonded to four others, no free electrons; graphite: each C bonded to three others in layers, with delocalised electrons that can move
steps: Diamond: each carbon forms four strong covalent bonds to four others in a giant tetrahedral lattice
All the outer electrons in diamond are used in bonding, so there are no mobile electrons and it does not conduct
Graphite: each carbon forms three covalent bonds in hexagonal layers, held to other layers by weak London forces
The fourth electron of each carbon in graphite is delocalised and moves along the layers, so graphite conducts
accept: diamond has a very high melting point because of the strong covalent bonds throughout
graphite is soft because the layers slide over each other
graphite conducts only parallel to the layers
graphene is a single layer of graphite

questions.question: Magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride. Explain why.
questions.answer: Mg2+ and O2- have higher charges and smaller radii than Na+ and Cl-, so the electrostatic attraction in the lattice is much stronger
steps: Both are giant ionic lattices, and melting needs the electrostatic attraction between ions to be overcome
Mg2+ and O2- have charges of 2+ and 2-, compared with 1+ and 1- for Na+ and Cl-
Mg2+ and O2- are smaller than Na+ and Cl-, so the attraction is stronger and more energy is needed to melt MgO
accept: the lattice energy of MgO is much greater than that of NaCl
the charge density of Mg2+ is greater than that of Na+
ionic radii: Mg2+ < Na+ and O2- < Cl-

questions.question: Lithium iodide has more covalent character than lithium fluoride. Explain why.
questions.answer: Li+ is small with a high charge density, and the large iodide ion is easily polarised, so the electron density is drawn towards the cation
steps: Li+ is small with a high charge density, so it has a strong polarising power
The large I- ion has an electron cloud that is easily distorted (highly polarisable)
Electron density is drawn into the region between the nuclei, so LiI has more covalent character than LiF
accept: F- is small and its electron cloud is held tightly, so it is hardly distorted
a small, highly charged cation and a large anion favour covalent character
the outer electrons of the larger anion are further from its nucleus, so they are more easily polarised

questions.question: An ammonia molecule reacts with a hydrogen ion to form an ammonium ion: NH3 + H+ -> NH4+. Explain what is meant by a dative covalent bond and show how one forms in this reaction.
questions.answer: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom; N donates its lone pair to H+
steps: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom
The nitrogen atom of NH3 donates its lone pair to the H+ ion (which has an empty orbital), forming the fourth N-H bond
accept: coordinate bond
dative bond shown as an arrow from N to H on a diagram
a lone pair on nitrogen is shared with the hydrogen ion

questions.question: The boiling points of the hydrogen halides are HF 293 K, HCl 188 K, HBr 207 K and HI 238 K. (a) Name the types of intermolecular force between HCl molecules.
questions.answer: London (dispersion) forces and permanent dipole-dipole forces
steps: London (dispersion) forces
Permanent dipole-dipole forces
accept: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces
van der Waals forces, if both types are described

questions.question: The boiling points of HCl, HBr and HI are 188 K, 207 K and 238 K respectively. (b) Explain why the boiling points increase from HCl to HI.
questions.answer: The number of electrons increases, so London forces get stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules
steps: The number of electrons increases from HCl to HI
So the London (dispersion) forces between the molecules are stronger
More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces, so the boiling point rises
accept: a larger electron cloud is more polarisable, giving larger instantaneous dipoles
the London forces outweigh the fall in bond polarity
the boiling point increases with relative molecular mass

questions.question: The boiling points of HCl and HF are 188 K and 293 K respectively. (c) Explain why the boiling point of HF is much higher than that of HCl.
questions.answer: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the forces between HCl molecules
steps: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Fluorine is small and very electronegative, so H has a large delta+ charge and F has a lone pair that attracts the H of another molecule
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the dipole-dipole and London forces in HCl, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules
accept: hydrogen bonding is a strong permanent dipole-dipole attraction
hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to F, O or N
more energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds than the forces between HCl molecules

questions.question: Hydrogen bonds also form between water molecules. (d) Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
questions.answer: In ice each water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in an open lattice, holding the molecules further apart than in liquid water
steps: In ice each water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in an open, regular lattice
So the molecules are further apart than in liquid water, giving a lower density
accept: the open lattice contains spaces
in liquid water some hydrogen bonds break and the molecules pack more closely
ice has a regular tetrahedral arrangement of molecules

questions.question: Which of these elements has the lowest melting point? A: phosphorus; B: sulfur; C: chlorine; D: silicon
questions.answer: C: chlorine
steps: Silicon is a giant covalent structure and has a very high melting point.
Phosphorus (P4), sulfur (S8) and chlorine (Cl2) are simple molecular, so only the weak London forces between molecules are overcome when they melt.
Cl2 has the smallest molecules and the fewest electrons, so it has the weakest London forces and the lowest melting point.

questions.question: Which ion has the smallest radius? A: O2-; B: F-; C: Na+; D: Mg2+
questions.answer: D: Mg2+
steps: All four ions have 10 electrons in the same shells (they are isoelectronic).
The ion with the most protons attracts these electrons most strongly, so it is the smallest.
Mg2+ has 12 protons, compared with 11 in Na+, 9 in F- and 8 in O2-, so Mg2+ has the smallest radius.

questions.question: Explain why there is a general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3 from sodium to argon.
questions.answer: Nuclear charge increases with the same shielding, so the atomic radius falls and the outer electrons are held more strongly
steps: The nuclear charge (number of protons) increases across the period
The electrons are added to the same shell, so the shielding is about the same and the atomic radius decreases
The outer electrons are held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one
accept: greater attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron
the effective nuclear charge increases across the period
the outer electron is removed from the same shell, so the shielding does not increase

questions.question: Explain the variation in melting point of the Period 3 elements: the increase from sodium to aluminium, the highest value at silicon, and the low values from phosphorus to argon.
questions.answer: Na to Al: stronger metallic bonding; Si: giant covalent lattice; P to Ar: weak London forces between small molecules or atoms
steps: Na, Mg and Al are metals, with a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
From Na to Al the ion charge and the number of delocalised electrons increase and the ions get smaller, so the metallic bonding is stronger and the melting point rises
Silicon has a giant covalent lattice with strong covalent bonds throughout, which need a great deal of energy to break, so it has the highest melting point
P4, S8 and Cl2 are simple molecules, so only the weak London forces between molecules are overcome and their melting points are low
S8 > P4 > Cl2 because larger molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces
Argon is monatomic with the weakest London forces, so it has the lowest melting point
accept: the charge density of the metal ion increases from Na to Al
silicon has a tetrahedral structure like diamond
no covalent bonds are broken when simple molecular substances melt
Mg has two delocalised electrons per atom and Al has three, compared with one for Na

questions.question: State and explain the trend in electronegativity across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
questions.answer: Electronegativity increases because the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases, so the bonding pair is attracted more strongly
steps: Electronegativity increases from sodium to chlorine
The nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases (shielding is about constant)
So the nucleus attracts the bonding pair of electrons more strongly
accept: the bonding electrons are closer to the nucleus
the effective nuclear charge increases
the outer shell stays the same (n = 3), so the shielding is about constant

questions.question: The electrical conductivity of the metals increases in the order sodium, magnesium, aluminium. Explain this trend.
questions.answer: The number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3), so more charge carriers move through the metal
steps: Metals conduct because delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Each Na atom provides 1 delocalised electron, each Mg atom 2 and each Al atom 3
There are more charge carriers per unit volume from Na to Al, so the conductivity increases
accept: delocalised electrons carry the charge when a potential difference is applied
the electron density in the metal lattice increases from Na to Al

questions.question: Atoms of the Period 3 elements all have their outer electrons in the third shell. (a) Explain why the atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine.
questions.answer: The nuclear charge increases while the shielding stays about the same, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly
steps: The number of protons (nuclear charge) increases from 11 in sodium to 17 in chlorine
The electrons are added to the same shell, so the shielding hardly changes
The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons increases, pulling them closer, so the atomic radius decreases
accept: the effective nuclear charge increases
the number of shells stays the same
a stronger force of attraction on the outer shell

questions.question: The sodium ion, Na+, is smaller than the sodium atom. (b) Explain why.
questions.answer: Na+ has lost the outer shell; the 11 protons now attract 10 electrons in two shells
steps: Na+ has lost its outer (3s) electron, so it has one fewer shell than the atom
The same nuclear charge (11+) attracts 10 electrons instead of 11, pulling them closer
accept: the ion has two shells and the atom three
less electron-electron repulsion in the ion

questions.question: The chloride ion, Cl-, is larger than the chlorine atom. (c) Explain why.
questions.answer: Cl- has the same nuclear charge but an extra electron, so there is more electron repulsion and the electron cloud expands
steps: Cl- has one more electron than Cl but the same number of protons
More electron-electron repulsion and a smaller nuclear attraction per electron, so the electron cloud expands
accept: the same nuclear charge (17+) acts on 18 electrons
the outer electrons repel one another more
the ratio of protons to electrons is smaller
